687.title: Greater than our heart (1 John 3:19–24)
687.hook: when our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart
687.howItsDone: Pastors and spiritual directors sometimes turn to 1 John 3:20 with people troubled by guilt or a harsh conscience, and some Christians memorize it as a comfort.

segments.voice: Yesterday: in deed and in truth, and the gut feeling love doesn't shut off. Your line was not in word only.

Some people have a prosecutor living in their head. It replays the awkward thing you said at the party. It reminds you of the mistake from ten years ago. It says, you call that love? After a passage about loving in deed and in truth, that voice can get loud: did I do enough? Have I ever really loved anyone that way? The writer of First John seems to know his own words can set it off. So right after asking for real, costly love, he turns to the reader whose heart is condemning them.

He says that by loving in deed we know we are of the truth, and "shall assure our hearts before him." Assure, here, means to calm, to persuade, to quiet down. Then the line: "For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things." Christians have heard this in two ways, and it's honest to say so. One reading hears comfort: your heart is a harsh judge, but not the final one. God is greater; he knows everything, including what you've forgotten, the good you did and the reasons you struggled, and, on this reading, he is merciful. Some older commentators heard a warning instead: if even your own heart condemns you, how much more does God, who knows all things? Both readings take God's knowledge seriously. Readers who favor comfort point to the paragraph's purpose, which is to settle the heart. Then: "Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God." Confidence is a word for freedom of speech, speaking openly, like a child who isn't afraid to ask. And he sums up the whole commandment in one sentence: "That we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another." Believe and love: two halves of one command. Last, he names how we know God lives in us: by the Spirit he has given us. In this letter, the heart is a witness, not the final judge.
screen: then, large: `GOD IS GREATER THAN OUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Let the inner prosecutor speak for a moment, and hear it out without arguing. Then imagine something bigger standing beside that voice, not to shout it down but to know more than it knows: the context it forgot, the good it skipped, the reasons it ignored. Breathe out, let your shoulders drop, and if you pray, bring the accusation to God and leave it there.
Confidence. First John's word for freedom of speech, speaking openly before God like a child unafraid to ask, when the heart does not condemn.
Your line: greater than your heart. Believe and love, one command in two halves. Until tomorrow.

688.title: Test the spirits (1 John 4:1–6)
688.hook: not every voice is from God; test it
688.howItsDone: Christians practice discernment by testing teachings against Scripture and the faith of the church, and some seek the help of a pastor, spiritual director or community; Ignatian discernment, from Ignatius of Loyola, is still taught today.

segments.voice: Yesterday: greater than our heart, and confidence, freedom to speak openly before God. Your line was greater than your heart.

Before there were labs, people tested gold by rubbing it on a dark stone and looking at the streak it left. Real gold left one color. Fakes left another. The stone was called a touchstone, and its lesson was simple: something can look exactly like gold and not be gold. Today the writer of First John turns brisk and practical: don't believe every voice. Test it.

In the King James Bible: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world." Try translates a Greek word also used for testing metal, an assayer's word. And he starts with beloved: not a cynic, but someone who loves his readers enough to want them not to be fooled. In his day, it seems, teachers were claiming the Spirit, and some said that Jesus didn't really come in a body. So his test fits his moment: "Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God." Remember the letter's opening: what our hands have handled. The test is whether a teaching holds on to a real, touchable Jesus. Then courage: "greater is he that is in you, than he that is in the world." The reader isn't small and helpless before every persuasive voice. And a sobering line: the world listens to its own. Popular doesn't mean true. Christians call this gift discernment; Paul lists the discerning of spirits among the Spirit's gifts. Churches have taught many ways to practice it. Catholic and Orthodox teaching weighs a claim against Scripture read with the church's tradition. Protestant teaching holds Scripture as the final test, often weighed with the counsel of a community. Ignatius of Loyola wrote rules for discerning the spirits that are still taught today. Each starts where the writer does: some voices sound like gold, so test them before trusting them.
screen: `GREATER IS HE THAT IS IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you accepted quickly this week, a headline, a rumor, a confident voice, even an inner voice about yourself, and hold it up like gold on a touchstone. Where did it come from, who benefits if you believe it, does it lead toward love or away from it? Don't rush to a verdict, and if you pray, ask for discernment.
Discernment. The gift of testing voices before trusting them, the way a touchstone tells real gold from fake.
Your line: like gold on a touchstone. Beloved comes first, then the test. Day six hundred eighty-eight, done.

689.title: God is love (1 John 4:7–12)
689.hook: whoever loves is born of God, for God is love
689.carry: love, and do what you will
689.howItsDone: 1 John 4:7–12 is read at some Christian weddings and funerals, and some churches teach children 'God is love' as a first, short summary of the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: test the spirits, and discernment, testing voices before trusting them. Your line was like gold on a touchstone.

Church signs. Wedding programs. Bumper stickers. A pillow stitched in a grandmother's living room. The same three words turn up on all of them, printed so often they can sound like wallpaper. But they began in this letter, and not as decoration. The writer has just told his readers to test every spirit, to watch for voices that sound right and aren't. Right after that warning, he sets down the line all those signs borrowed. Today, those three words where they actually live.

In the King James Bible: "Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God." Love comes from God, the way light comes from the sun. Then: "He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love." Notice the order. God is love, not love is God; in the Greek, the grammar makes God the subject. The writer isn't saying that whatever we feel as love is divine. He's saying love belongs to God's very nature. And what does that love look like? "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins." The love starts on God's side. Propitiation is a heavy word: the offering that makes things right between us and God. Christians explain how that works in different ways, but they agree on the direction: love reaching first. Then a startling line: "No man hath seen God at any time." Nobody. Yet: "If we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us." In the writer's telling, the unseen God is found, in a sense, wherever people love. Centuries later, Augustine preached a series of sermons on this letter. In one he said, in Latin, dilige, et quod vis fac: love, and do what you will. He didn't mean anything goes. He meant that if love is the root within, what grows from it will be good.
screen: `GOD IS LOVE, NOT LOVE IS GOD.`
`HE LOVED US FIRST, AND SENT HIS SON.`
`NO ONE HAS SEEN GOD. LOVE SHOWS HIM.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you love with a few conditions attached, if they'd only call more, if they'd say sorry first, and picture their face. Gently set the conditions down one at a time, like taking stones out of your pockets, and notice what's left. If you pray, hold their name before God, just as they are.
Agape. Greek for self-giving love: First John's claim that God is love, not that love is God, and that love belongs to God's very nature.
Your line: love, and do what you will. Three words, back where they began. Take care until tomorrow.

690.title: Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:13–18)
690.hook: there is no fear in love
690.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize 1 John 4:18 and pray it in times of anxiety, and pastors often use it to distinguish reverent awe of God from dread of punishment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: God is love, and agape, love that reaches first. Your line was love, and do what you will.

Watch a toddler at the playground. They run off, climb something too high, look around, and find their parent's face. If the face is there, they go a little farther. If it isn't, panic. Psychologists call this a secure base: a child who's sure of being loved explores more, not less. Fear shrinks the world; love widens it. The writer of First John never read a psychology textbook, but he says something very close, in one short verse about what love does to fear.

First he repeats a great line and adds to it. In the King James Bible: "God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him." Dwelleth means to live in, to make your home in. Love isn't only something God does; it's a place you can live. Then the verse: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love." Three things to notice. Perfect doesn't mean flawless; the Greek means complete, full-grown, mature. Casteth out is a strong verb, the word for throwing something out the door. Love doesn't negotiate with fear; it shows it out. And fear hath torment: the word can also mean punishment. The fear he means is the dread of being punished, the fear of a child who expects to be hit. A fair question: doesn't the Bible also talk about the fear of the Lord? It does, often. Many Christian teachers distinguish two kinds of fear. One is reverence, awe before something holy, like standing at the edge of the ocean. The other is dread, cringing before a punisher. The writer seems to mean the second. Reverence can stay; dread is what love throws out. And the context is judgment day: he says we can have boldness even then. Not because we're flawless, but because, as he says, as he is, so are we in this world.
screen: then, large: `THERE IS NO FEAR IN LOVE.`

segments.voice: Name one fear that has been with you lately, being left, getting it wrong, getting sick, and ask it gently what it's afraid will happen to you. Then picture beside it the face of someone who loves you, or, if you pray, the love of God, and let love stand in the same room with the fear without arguing. Notice which one takes up more space after a minute.
Torment. The dread that perfect, full-grown love throws out the door, First John says, so that people need not live in fear of punishment.
Your line: no fear in love. Full-grown love leaves room to explore. Day six hundred ninety.

691.title: We love because (1 John 4:19–21)
691.hook: we love him because he first loved us
691.howItsDone: 1 John 4:19 is a short verse some Christians memorize as a summary of their faith, and some churches teach it to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: perfect love casts out fear, the torment of dread. Your line was no fear in love.

Stand at the edge of a canyon and say nothing, and the canyon says nothing back. Call out, and a moment later the rock answers in your own voice. An echo never goes first. It only exists because something reached it. Today the writer of First John asks where love comes from in the first place. The passage is three verses long, and its first line is about exactly that: which love comes first, and which one answers.

In the King James Bible: "We love him, because he first loved us." Short enough to carry, and some readers hear the whole letter in it. In the writer's telling, our love is a response, and God's love goes first. Some readers also notice that the line still stands without the word him: we love, because he first loved us. Read that way, it's not only that we love God because God loved us. We love at all, anyone at all, because we were loved first. Then the writer makes it concrete, and uncomfortable: "If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" He's not being harsh for fun. God is invisible. Your brother is right in front of you, irritating habits and all. If you can't love the one you can see, the claim to love the one you can't is hard to believe. It's a test anyone can turn on themselves, and the letter doesn't pretend anyone passes it cleanly. Maybe that's why it comes right after the line about who loved first. Then: "And this commandment have we from him, That he who loveth God love his brother also." One commandment, pointing two ways: up toward the God no one has seen, and sideways toward the brother in the next chair. The letter has circled this from its first page, light, children, deeds, fear, and here it lands.
screen: then, large: `BECAUSE HE FIRST LOVED US.`

segments.voice: For a minute, don't try to love anyone; remember being loved instead, a parent's voice, a friend who stayed, a stranger's kindness on a bad day, and stay in that one memory without hurrying to pay it back. If you pray, receive God's love the same way, with nothing to do but be loved. Only at the end, notice whether anything in you wants to answer.
Echo. The hook's picture for our love: it never goes first, First John says, because he first loved us, and we only answer back.
Your line: he first loved us. Our love is the echo. That's day six hundred ninety-one.

692.title: That you may know (1 John 5)
692.hook: the letter ends: little children, keep yourselves from idols
692.howItsDone: Some Christians read 1 John 5:13 as a word of assurance, and in teaching and preaching the letter's last line about idols is sometimes applied to anything, not only statues, that takes God's place in a life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: we love because he first loved us, our love an echo. Your line was he first loved us.

Some letters bury the point in the middle. This one saves it for the end. In the last chapter, the writer gives what some readers take as his reason for writing all of it. And he signs off with a line that seems to come out of nowhere. Not grace be with you. Not peace. Just this: little children, keep yourselves from idols. No explanation, and then amen.

The chapter opens with love in practice. In the King James Bible: "For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous." Not grievous: not a crushing load. And: "this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith." Then the purpose of the whole letter, in verse thirteen: "These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life." That ye may know: not hope, not guess, not lie awake wondering. Some readers hear the Greek verb as settled knowing, the kind you don't keep checking. After page after page of tests, you might expect anxiety; the writer says he wrote so they could stop wondering and rest. A note for anyone comparing Bibles. In the King James Bible, verse seven has a line about three that bear record in heaven: the Father, the Word and the Holy Ghost. Some modern translations leave that line out or put it in a footnote, and their notes explain why. Churches that teach the Trinity draw it from many passages and the early creeds, not from this one verse. Then the ending: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols." Scholars aren't sure what he had in mind. Maybe the temple statues in a city like Ephesus, where tradition places the elder. Maybe the false pictures of God the letter has warned about. Maybe anything that quietly takes God's place. The letter doesn't say. It leaves the line ringing, like a parent calling after you at the door: take care of yourselves.
screen: `WRITTEN SO YOU CAN KNOW, NOT GUESS.`

segments.voice: In the wider sense some Christian teachers use, an idol is anything sitting in the center where something truer belongs: your phone, someone's approval, money, a grudge, a plan for how life has to go. Name one gently, like a houseguest who has stayed too long, and let each breath move it an inch from the center. If you pray, rest on the old line from Psalm 46: be still, and know that I am God.
Idols. The strange parting shot that ends First John: keep yourselves from idols, after a letter written so its readers could know, not guess, that they have life.
Your line: keep yourselves from idols. A parting word, like a parent's at the door. See you tomorrow.

693.title: Face to face (2 and 3 John)
693.hook: two postcards from the elder: I'd rather not write with ink, but talk face to face
693.carry: a tone, a hand on the shoulder
693.howItsDone: In Christian communities, hospitality and visiting, especially of the sick, the homebound and travelers, are a traditional part of life together, and 3 John's praise of Gaius is sometimes read as a picture of that welcome.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of First John, written so you may know, and its parting line. Your line was keep yourselves from idols.

Count the times this week you texted someone you could have called, or called someone you could have visited. No judgment; it's how a lot of life works now. Long ago, a church leader who calls himself simply the elder felt the pull the other way. Two of his notes survive in the Bible, Second and Third John, each only a page or so long. Both end with almost the same line: I have more to say, but I'd rather not say it in ink. I'd rather come and talk to you face to face.
screen: `I'D RATHER NOT WRITE IT IN INK.`

segments.voice: Second John is addressed "unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth." Nobody knows who she is. She might be a woman who hosted a church in her home. Some readers think the elect lady names a whole congregation, with her children as its members. The note repeats the heart of First John: love one another, walk in his commandments, and beware teachers who deny that Jesus came in the flesh. Third John is a personal note to "the wellbeloved Gaius." There's praise for Gaius, who opened his home to traveling teachers. There's a complaint about a man named Diotrephes, "who loveth to have the preeminence among them," and who turned those travelers away. And a good word for someone called Demetrius. Then both notes end the same way. In the King James Bible, Second John says: "Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full." The Greek is more bodily than the English: not face to face but mouth to mouth, stoma pros stoma. The elder knew what ink can't carry: a tone, a hand on the shoulder, the look on someone's face when they finally understand. That closes a week about love, from greater than your heart to face to face, ending with an elder who'd rather show up in person.
